intro: Sardinia's seven trees are spread across the island and only a car links them. Two stand a few metres apart at Santu Baltolu near Luras in Gallura, and one, S'Ozzastru, is the oldest living tree in Italy. Two more sit around Baunei on the Ogliastra coast, a cedar grows inland at Laconi, and two great oaks stand in the mountains between: the cork oak of Sa Tuppa near Orune, which a Sardinian botanist calls the most imposing on the island, and a downy oak in a wood of two hundred giants at Su Fundale. None of it is an afternoon.
meta_description: Sardinia's seven remarkable trees, including S'Ozzastru near Luras, the oldest living tree in Italy at somewhere between 2,500 and 4,000 years.
question_meta: Sardinia's oldest tree is S'Ozzastru near Luras, a wild olive estimated at 2,500 to 4,000 years and the oldest living tree in Italy.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Sardinia, and in Italy, is S'Ozzastru, a wild olive at Santu Baltolu di Carana outside Luras in Gallura. Its age is genuinely contested: the University of Sassari estimates 2,500 to 4,000 years, the visitor site that manages it says 3,000 to 4,000, and the botanist Bruno Peyronel once proposed more than 5,000, a figure flagged as having no scientific data behind it. Every serious estimate lands in the thousands, which settles the ranking without settling the number.
question_context: Sardinia holds the oldest tree in Italy and cannot tell you how old it is. S'Ozzastru, the wild olive at Santu Baltolu di Carana outside Luras, has been estimated at 2,500 to 4,000 years by the University of Sassari and at 3,000 to 4,000 by the visitor site that manages it, while a botanist's guess of more than 5,000 circulates with nothing behind it. The spread is not sloppiness. Ancient olives hollow out and lose their heartwood, which removes the material a ring count or a radiocarbon test would use, so every figure for a tree like this is a model rather than a measurement. What can be measured is the trunk: 11.5 metres around, on a tree 14 metres tall with a crown of about 21 metres, protected as a national natural monument since 1991. The companion olivastro a few metres away is put at roughly 2,000 years by secondary sources that show no working. The olive at Santa Maria Navarrese is called millenario by the regional forestry agency and about 2,000 years by local press. The trees at San Pietro in Golgo carry no age at all, and the cedar at Laconi is much the youngest here.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sardinia?
faq.a: S'Ozzastru, the wild olive at Santu Baltolu di Carana outside Luras in Gallura. Estimates run from 2,500 to 4,000 years and it is generally called the oldest living tree in Italy. It is a national natural monument, designated in 1991, and its trunk measures 11.5 metres around.

faq.q: Why can nobody agree how old S'Ozzastru is?
faq.a: Ancient olives hollow out and lose their heartwood, so there is no continuous core to count rings in and nothing for radiocarbon dating to work on. Every figure is therefore a growth model rather than a measurement. The University of Sassari gives 2,500 to 4,000 years, the managing visitor site 3,000 to 4,000, and an old speculation of over 5,000 has no scientific data supporting it.

faq.q: Do you need a car, and how far apart are these trees?
faq.a: A car, and they are a long way apart. The two olivastri at Santu Baltolu stand a few metres from each other near Luras in the north. Santa Maria Navarrese and the Golgo plateau are around Baunei on the east coast, roughly 150 kilometres south, and about 25 minutes apart from each other. Laconi is inland again, and the two great oaks at Orune and Su Fundale lie in the mountains in between. Treat this as two or three separate days rather than one drive.

faq.q: Can you visit S'Ozzastru at any time of year?
faq.a: No. The grove at Santu Baltolu is a managed site with a ticket office, open from 1 April to 2 November with guided visits from 10:30 and a fee of around 5 euro. The other trees on this list are free and open at all hours.

trees.name: S'Ozzastru

location.address: Localita Santu Baltolu di Carana, Luras (near Lake Liscia)

trees.story:
Italy's oldest living tree has an age nobody can pin down within fifteen centuries. S'Ozzastru is a wild olive at Santu Baltolu di Carana, outside Luras in the granite hills of Gallura, and Sardinians call it su babbu mannu, the great father, or the patriarch of all wild olives. The University of Sassari puts it between 2,500 and 4,000 years old. The site that manages it says 3,000 to 4,000. The Piedmontese botanist Bruno Peyronel once suggested more than 5,000, a figure that comes with no scientific data behind it and which he applied to other trees just as freely. All of them are estimates, because an ancient olive hollows out and loses the heartwood any ring count would need, and this trunk is hollow.

The measurements are firmer, and they are what makes the visit. The trunk runs 11.5 metres around, the tree stands 14 metres tall and the crown spreads about 21 metres, which is a wild olive behaving like an oak. Sardinia declared it a national natural monument in 1991.

It is not a tree you stumble on. The grove is a managed site now, with a ticket office, a path and a guide, open from April to early November, and a second ancient olivastro stands a few metres along the same walk.
trees.access: Paid entry, 5 EUR, guided visit only. Open 1 April to 2 November, visits from 10:30. Managed tourist site with ticket office, picnic area and Lake Liscia boat trips.
trees.transport: No public transport; a car is the realistic way, roughly 20 minutes from Luras or Tempio Pausania. On-site parking at the visitor centre.
trees.notes: THE anchor tree of the whole island page: Italy's oldest tree and one of Europe's oldest, a National Natural Monument since 1991 (Decreto Assessorato Difesa Ambiente, L.R. 31/89). Local Sardinian name means 'the patriarch of all wild olives' or su babbu mannu (the great father). AGE IS CONTESTED and deliberately unresolved: University of Sassari estimates 2,500-4,000 years (cited by it.wikipedia.org); the tree's own visitor site says 3,000-4,000 years; Bruno Peyronel speculated it could exceed 5,000, but Wikipedia flags this explicitly as having 'no scientific data to support it', same as for other trees Peyronel guessed at. Olives cannot be ring-dated in the ordinary way: the trunk hollows out and loses its heartwood as it ages, which is why every age here is an estimate and why the estimates disagree by thousands of years. Measurements corroborate across independent sources: MASAF register girth 1154cm vs Wikipedia's 11.5m; both give height 14m; Wikipedia adds crown diameter 21m. Actively managed and promoted as a living tourist attraction as of 2026 (site content dated June 2026), no death or decline reported. A second, smaller olivastro stands a few metres away (sar_002) in the same protected grove, 'Olivastri Millenari di Santu Baltolu'.
trees.verify_notes: Height 14.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk, 11.5 metres round, and a crown spreading about 21 metres like an oak rather than an olive. It stands at Santu Baltolu di Carana, near Lake Liscia.

trees.name: The Second Olivastro of Santu Baltolu

location.address: Localita Santu Baltolu di Carana, Luras, standing a few metres from S'Ozzastru

trees.story:
This tree has no name of its own, which is the clearest measure of what standing next to S'Ozzastru costs a tree. Almost anywhere else on Sardinia it would be the reason people came. Here it is the one they photograph on the way back to the car. The second olivastro of Santu Baltolu is a wild olive with a trunk 5.4 metres around, less than half its neighbour's 11.5, and that ratio is the only thing that makes it read as small. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists it separately, on its own sheet, and it shares the 1991 natural monument designation that protects the grove.

Its age is the loosest figure on this page. Sardinian sources put it at around 2,000 years and none of them shows any working at all, so read that as a guess in roughly the right neighbourhood rather than a measurement. Nobody has taken a proper dating to it. If you have seen one published, tell us.

What is not in doubt is the species and the setting. Wild olives are what the Mediterranean grew before anyone cultivated anything, and two of them at this size, in the same thin Gallurese soil, on the same short guided walk, is the genuinely rare part.
trees.access: Same paid site as S'Ozzastru: 5 EUR guided visit, open 1 April to 2 November from 10:30.
trees.transport: Same as S'Ozzastru, on the same visitor path a few metres from the main tree. A car is the realistic way, roughly 20 minutes from Luras or Tempio Pausania.

photo.note: fine olivastro but the title names the plurimillenario, likely S'Ozzastru rather than our second tree at the same site

trees.notes: Companion tree to S'Ozzastru, individually registered by MASAF at 540cm girth (well under S'Ozzastru's 1154cm) but a genuinely ancient wild olive in its own right, part of the same protected grove and the same 1991 natural-monument designation. Secondary sources describe it as standing 'a few metres away' from the patriarch and give a rough estimate of about 2,000 years, but none of them shows working for that figure, so it is repeated as vaguely as given rather than sharpened; no dedicated proper name found beyond 'the second olivastro' in the sources checked, unlike S'Ozzastru, which has its own Sardinian name. Same access and same alive-now evidence as sar_001, since both stand in the actively managed visitor grove.
trees.verify_notes: Height 8.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk 5.4 metres round, less than half the girth of its unmissable neighbour S'Ozzastru a few metres away. It stands on the same guided walk at Santu Baltolu di Carana.

trees.name: The Olivastro of Santa Maria Navarrese

location.address: Piazza Principessa di Navarra, next to the church of Santa Maria di Navarra (1502), Santa Maria Navarrese, Baunei

trees.story:
Somebody tried to burn this tree down in the early 1960s and the fire scars are still on the trunk. The olivastro of Santa Maria Navarrese survived the arson and is still rated in good condition by the region's own foresters, despite a trunk that is partly hollow, which is the usual state of an olive this old.

It stands in the village square beside the church of Santa Maria di Navarra, built in 1502 and, on every estimate anyone has offered, many centuries younger than the tree next to it. Sardinia's forestry agency measures the trunk at 8.40 metres around at 1.3 metres up, with a crown of 9 to 10 metres. The national register gives a slightly larger figure, 9.05 metres, probably taken at a different point on the trunk; nobody has reconciled the two.

The age is stated loosely on purpose. The regional agency calls it millenario, at least a thousand years, and gives no number. Local press quotes botanists at about 2,000. Neither figure comes with any working attached, and no one has published a dating.

The Region declared it a natural monument in January 1994, along with the other old olives, carobs and hackberries in the same square. It is free, in the open, and a short walk up from the harbour.
trees.access: Free, standing in a public square beside the church, open at all times.
trees.transport: In the village of Santa Maria Navarrese, a coastal frazione of Baunei; walkable from the harbour and beach. A car is the realistic way to reach the village itself, about 150 km south of the Luras trees.
trees.notes: NOTE: the original lead named this a Sughera (cork oak); it is not, it is a wild olive (olivastro), corrected during verification. Stands beside the 1502 church of Santa Maria di Navarra, in the square that gives the village its name. Regione Sardegna's own forestry agency (SardegnaForeste, citing 'I monumenti naturali della Sardegna', Barroccu/Gentileschi, Carlo Delfino Editore 1996) gives the official measurement: crown 9-10m, trunk circumference 8.40m at 1.30m height, vegetative state 'good' despite a partly hollow trunk and visible fire scars from an arson attack in the early 1960s. MASAF's own register gives a slightly larger girth, 905cm, for the same locality, most likely a different measurement point or a later remeasurement; both recorded, not resolved. Declared Natural Monument by the Region of Sardinia in January 1994 together with other ancient olives, carobs and hackberries in the same square (MASAF separately lists a Bagolaro at 367cm and a Carrubo at 332cm in the same piazza, sheets 02 and 03/A722/OG/20, not separate entries: less individually remarkable and clearly secondary to the olive in every source). Alive as of 2023 per vistanet.it, present tense. Age: SardegnaForeste calls it 'millenario' (at least a thousand years) without a number; vistanet.it (2023) cites unnamed botanical experts at 'circa duemila anni'. No dendrological working shown for either figure; reported as given.
trees.verify_notes: Height 10.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by fire scars still visible on the trunk, 8.4 metres round, from an arson attempt in the early 1960s. It stands in the village square beside the 1502 church of Santa Maria di Navarra.

trees.name: The Ancient Trees of San Pietro in Golgo
trees.species: Wild Olive and Mediterranean Hackberry (Olea europaea var. sylvestris and Celtis australis)

location.address: Beside the rural church of San Pietro (San Pietro in Golgo), Altopiano del Golgo, Baunei

trees.story:
Nobody has ever put an age to these trees, and up on the Golgo plateau that feels about right. A small rural church, San Pietro, sits 13 kilometres above Baunei on a lava tableland, and it is flanked by aged wild olives and hackberries. Two of them are registered individually in Italy's national inventory of monumental trees: a wild olive with a trunk 5.68 metres around and a hackberry at 5.25 metres, standing effectively on the same spot. Sardinia's own forestry service describes the church in exactly those words, fiancheggiata da annosi olivastri e bagolari, flanked by aged wild olives and hackberries.

There is no age field anywhere for either of them and no source ventures a guess, so this page does not either. If somebody has measured them, send it to us.

The setting does most of the work. Shepherds' stone huts, the cumbessias, stand alongside the church and still fill for the annual festival, and the Su Sterru sinkhole opens in the ground nearby, which is what brings most people up the road in the first place. The long-distance Selvaggio Blu route passes through. There is no gate and no fee, and the church itself is the place to stand.
verified_sources: https://www.fotosardegna.it/chiesa-di-san-pietro-in-golgo/ (a hackberry and a wild olive, both over 200 years old, stand in front of the church walls and are listed among Italy's monumental trees)
trees.access: Free, a working rural church on open plateau land reached by the paved road up from Baunei (about 13km); also a stop on the Selvaggio Blu and other hiking routes. No gate, no fee found in any source checked.
trees.transport: No public transport; a car is the realistic way, roughly 20 to 25 minutes up the plateau road from Baunei. Frequently visited alongside the Su Sterru sinkhole nearby.
trees.notes: Treated as one ensemble entry: a wild olive (girth 568cm, MASAF sheet 05/A722/OG/20) and a hackberry/bagolaro (girth 525cm, sheet 04/A722/OG/20) standing together at the same tiny rural church, 13km from Baunei on the Golgo plateau, both individually MASAF-registered at essentially the same coordinates. SardegnaForeste's own regional page (independent of MASAF, describing the wider Golgo/Su Sterru natural monument) confirms in its own words that the church 'e fiancheggiata da annosi olivastri e bagolari', which is the one collectible point here: the little basalt church itself, not a wood. This is a remote pastoral site (shepherds' cumbessias/staulus alongside it, used for an annual festival) rather than a town square, so location_precision is approximate: the two MASAF points sit almost on top of each other and are very likely accurate, but there is no independent tree-level photo or aerial confirmation, only the register plus a regional description of the site as a whole. No age given anywhere; MASAF has no age field and no secondary source ventures one, so this ships with age_estimate 'not documented' rather than guessed. No death or decline signal found; the site is an active, currently promoted natural monument and pilgrimage/festival site.
trees.verify_notes: Height 20.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the aged wild olive and hackberry flanking the rural church, trunks 5.68 and 5.25 metres round. They stand beside San Pietro on the Golgo plateau above Baunei.

location_site.name: Church of San Pietro in Golgo (the ground in front of the church walls)

trees.name: The Cedar of Parco Aymerich
trees.age_estimate: roughly 190 years, if the 1835 planting date is accurate

location.address: Parco Aymerich, Laconi (public park, free entry)

trees.story:
A Sardinian marquis with a botany habit is said to have planted this cedar in 1835, when it was already six years old, as one of the first Cedars of Lebanon brought into Europe. That account runs consistently through Sardinian sources, but the page citing it most directly is now dead, so treat the date as reported rather than proved. What two official bodies do confirm is the setting. Ignazio Aymerich began laying out this park from 1830 and filled it with rare exotic species, and the regional forestry agency that runs the park today calls the cedar imponente and the oldest of its kind on the island.

Take the 1835 date at face value and the tree is about 190 years old, which by cedar standards is early middle age; the species routinely runs past a thousand in its native Lebanon. The national register measures it at 4.4 metres round and 29 metres tall.

One detail nobody mentions: an oriental plane a few metres away is actually the thicker tree, at 4.5 metres round. The cedar is simply the one everybody comes for. The park is free and open daily under the regional forestry agency, a short walk from Laconi's Piazza Marconi and the Palazzo Aymerich down to the Su Acili entrance.

best_time.label: autumn, when the upright cones stand along the branches

trees.access: Free, open daily roughly 8:00-20:00 depending on season, managed by SardegnaForeste, the regional forestry agency. Public urban park, no restriction.
trees.transport: Short walk from Laconi town centre (Piazza Marconi / Palazzo Aymerich) to the main entrance at Su Acili. Laconi is inland in the Sarcidano hills, so a car is the realistic way to reach the town.
trees.notes: FLAGGED, weaker sourcing than the other four: the specific planting story (planted 1835, already 6 years old, one of the first Cedars of Lebanon introduced to Europe) appears consistently across several independent Sardinian travel/history sites (informati-sardegna.it, thewom.travel, and others surfaced by search), but the page most directly citing it (alberimonumentali.info) 404'd on fetch and informati-sardegna.it is JS-rendered so its exact wording could not be pulled directly, only via search snippets. What IS independently confirmed by two official sources fetched directly: the park was created from 1830 by Marchese Ignazio Aymerich, a botany enthusiast who planted rare exotic species (APGI, the Italian Parks and Gardens Association, and SardegnaForeste, the regional forestry agency that manages the park); the cedar itself is called 'imponente' and the oldest/tallest Cedar of Lebanon in Sardinia in multiple sources; MASAF registers it at 440cm girth, 29m height. If the 1835 planting date is right this is a genuine documented-planting-date estimate, not a bridge claim, because multiple sources tie the date to THIS specific tree rather than just the park; but given the sourcing gap, the age band is soft and the story says so. The same small park also holds a MASAF-registered Platanus orientalis at 450cm girth (sheet 04/E400/OR/20, slightly thicker than the cedar) a few metres away, mentioned in the story as context, not delivered as a separate entry. No decline or death signal found; the park is an actively maintained, visited public site. best_time set from data/phenology/cedar-of-lebanon.json, which rates the autumn cones 'striking'.
trees.verify_notes: Height 29.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 4.4 metres round and 29 metres tall, said to have been planted by a Sardinian marquis in 1835. It stands in Parco Aymerich, Laconi.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of Sa Tuppa

location.address: Sa Tuppa, on the plateau about 7 km west of Orune, Province of Nuoro

trees.story:
This tree is still harvested for its cork, and it has kept its shape anyway. The botanist Ignazio Camarda, who catalogued Sardinia's great trees and old forests in a 2020 book, calls the cork oak of Sa Tuppa the most imposing and best preserved in Sardinia, a tree that could stand as the symbol of its species. The cork comes off regularly, as it does from the working trees around it, and the trunk carries the swellings the cutting leaves behind, yet it has stayed whole and regular.

Camarda measures it at 6.5 metres round at chest height and 9.7 metres at the base, 20 metres tall, and puts its age at 200 to 300 years. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists it too, at 6.2 metres round.

It grows at about 740 metres up, in a clearing kept for free-range grazing, mostly sheep, which sometimes rest in its shade at midday, the spot Sardinians call a meriagu. Branches brought down by wind and snow lie under the crown, but Camarda records the tree as in very good health. Around it the whole Orune plateau is wooded pasture and cork forest, so dense and so full of big trees that he treats the area itself as a monumental cork oak forest.
verified_sources: Ignazio Camarda, Grandi alberi e foreste vetuste della Sardegna: biodiversità, luoghi, paesaggio, storia (2020), entry sent by Luisa Carta, curator of the Orto Botanico of the University of Sassari, 2026-10-13
data/registers/italy-masaf.json (sheet 02/G147/NU/20, Orune, Sa Tuppa: Quercus suber, girth 620 cm, height 21.5 m, 9 m from our pin)
https://www.komoot.com/guide/3906774/natural-monuments-around-orune (a 'Cork Oak Tree' loop from Nuoro to Orune, so visitors ride out to it)
trees.access: Free, no ticket. Stands in open wooded pasture used for free-range grazing on the Orune plateau, about 740 m up. No facilities, and sheep may be in the field.
trees.transport: Car only. Orune lies north-east of Nuoro; the tree is at Sa Tuppa on the plateau about 7 km west of the village.

trees.name: The Downy Oak of Su Fundale

location.address: Su Fundale, on the provincial road from Cantoniera Pira Onni to Talana, Province of Nuoro (Ogliastra)

trees.story:
This oak is one of more than two hundred. At Su Fundale, high in the mountains of Ogliastra, a wood of downy oaks runs for 25 to 30 hectares, and every trunk in it is about a metre across or more. The botanist Ignazio Camarda, who catalogued Sardinia's great trees in 2020, calls it an extraordinary sequence of big trees, with unusual bases and roots often half bare above the ground. Many carry the marks of lightning, some have dead tops, others full and healthy crowns.

This is the one Italy's national register of monumental trees lists by itself: 6.4 metres round and 19 metres tall, at about 930 metres up. Camarda puts its age at 300 to 400 years. For the wood as a whole he reads 400 to 500 years from the size of fallen and cut stumps and from growth rings only a few millimetres wide. A holm oak 5.25 metres round, also on the register, stands about 50 metres away.

Holm oak forest closes the wood in to the south and heath to the north, and among the oaks grow wild pear, prickly juniper and the rarer Montpellier maple. The provincial road towards Talana runs straight through the stand, so these trees are a stop on the drive rather than a hike: where the road crosses the wood, the trunks are all around you.
verified_sources: Ignazio Camarda, Grandi alberi e foreste vetuste della Sardegna: biodiversità, luoghi, paesaggio, storia (2020), entry sent by Luisa Carta, curator of the Orto Botanico of the University of Sassari, 2026-10-13

trees.access: Free, no ticket. The oak wood at Su Fundale is crossed by the provincial road from Cantoniera Pira Onni to Talana, so the trees stand in open forest beside the road.
trees.transport: Car only. Su Fundale is in the mountains of Ogliastra, on the provincial road from Villagrande Strisaili or Passo Correboi through Cantoniera Pira Onni towards Talana.
